In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

authors.name: Han Wu, Alex Chan, Ekin Can Erkus, Tousif Rahman, Rishad Shafik

papers.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
papers.summary: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.

authors.name: Keegan Wang, Anantika Mannby

papers.title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
papers.summary: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.

authors.name: Ramesh Arvind Naagarajan

papers.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
papers.summary: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.

authors.name: Angelo Ziletti

papers.title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
papers.summary: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

authors.name: Soheil Abbasloo, Peng Cheng

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
papers.summary: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

authors.name: Shiye Su, Xiaohan Wang, Ludwig Schmidt, Serena Yeung-Levy

papers.title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
papers.summary: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

authors.name: Jiaxin Huang, Chengxing Lin, Xiaoyu Luo, Sirui Chen, Jingyu Guo, Aolin Li, Kairui Chen, Rui Zhen, Cheng Wen, Kerui Gu, Shunyao Wang, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang

papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.summary: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.

authors.name: Muhammed Izzet Sezer, Sevval Belkis Dikkaya

papers.title: CoTTAGE: An Explainable Judge for Text-to-Audio Generation
papers.summary: Rapid progress in text-to-audio (TTA) generation demands reliable and explainable automatic evaluation. However, existing metrics fail to simultaneously deliver high correlation with human judgments and meaningful, audio-grounded explanations, forcing reliance on labor-intensive human evaluation that bottlenecks model development iteration. To address this, we propose CoTTAGE, a reasoning-based evaluator for text relevance (REL) and audio quality (OVL). Following a reason-then-predict paradigm, CoTTAGE first generates an audio-grounded rationale to diagnose errors before predicting scores. Supported by over 10K newly collected human OVL annotations, CoTTAGE is first trained via supervised fine-tuning and then refined with reinforcement learning using a Thurstone-based preference objective that converts sampled score distributions into pairwise preference probabilities and rewards agreement with rankings derived from human judgments. Across six benchmarks spanning REL and OVL, CoTTAGE achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments while producing human-preferred explanations to accelerate TTA development.

authors.name: Yu-Xiang Lin, Yun-Man Hsu, Bo-Ru Lu, Kuan-Po Huang, Wenze Ren, Ming-To Chuang, Chun-Yi Kuan, Jiawei Du, Byeonggeun Kim, Qingming Tang, Chieh-Chi Kao, Ankur Gandhe, Chao Wang, Hung-yi Lee

papers.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
papers.summary: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.

authors.name: Lucas Senos Coutinho, Matheus Vargas, Pedro Teixeira, Heudson Tosta Mirandola, Ori Rottenstreich, Priscila Machado Vieira Lima, Leandro Santiago, Daniel Sadoc Menasche

papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.summary: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

authors.name: Christopher Malili

papers.title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
papers.summary: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.

authors.name: Andre Albrecht, Enzo Morosini Frazzon, Leandro C. Coelho, Bruno Vieira

papers.title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
papers.summary: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

authors.name: Kate Yuan, Rohan Alur, Manish Raghavan, Devavrat Shah

papers.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
papers.summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

authors.name: Prabod Rathnayaka, Isura Manchanayake, Srikandabala Kogul, Steve Siu, Fabian Waschkowski, Lukas Wesemann

papers.title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
papers.summary: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

authors.name: Takeshi Onishi, Hiroya Makino, Takahiro Yamaguchi, Hiroyuki Sakai

papers.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
papers.summary: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

authors.name: Suhaas Garre, Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen

papers.title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
papers.summary: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

authors.name: Megan Wei, Damon Pham, John Cayley, Ellie Pavlick

papers.title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
papers.summary: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

authors.name: Ibrahim Memon, Armin Karamzade, M. Hanif Jhaveri, Roy Fox

papers.title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
papers.summary: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.

authors.name: Tie-Yun Li, Hao-Ran Wang, Chao Wang, Zhiyong Yin, Yiming Xu, Zhenwei Cai, Li Li, Rongzhi Lin, Feng-Lei Fan

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
papers.summary: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

authors.name: Mohamed Abdallah Salem

papers.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
papers.summary: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

authors.name: Mizuho Okitani, Yoshinobu Hagiwara

papers.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

authors.name: Lihuan Li, Ruiyi Yang, Jiru Wang, Yifan Duan, Xiachong Lin, Hao Xue, Yang Song, Flora Salim

papers.title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
papers.summary: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

authors.name: Xingyi Li, Jiahao Yang, Yiqin Zhu, Jingwen Ye, Yang Sun, Weidong Zhang

papers.title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
papers.summary: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.

authors.name: Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi

papers.title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
papers.summary: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

authors.name: Bo Qin, Zeyun Yang, Qiaofei Xue, Yanan Ding, Jinyu Wang, Chaopeng Ji, Shijin Yuan, Bin Mu, Wansuo Duan, Guokun Dai, Mu Mu, Yi Deng

papers.title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
papers.summary: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.

authors.name: Rajarshi Roy, Xiaowei Huang

papers.title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
papers.summary: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.

authors.name: Astarag Mohapatra

papers.title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
papers.summary: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE

authors.name: Kailai Sun, Zijie Gao, Mingyi He, Can Rong, Alok Prakash, Baoshen Guo, Shenhao Wang, Jinhua Zhao

papers.title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.

authors.name: Tiantong Wang, Zhiren Gong, Yixin Wang, Tiantong Wu, Wei Yang Bryan Lim

papers.title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
papers.summary: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.

authors.name: Olaf Hellwich, Moritz Heine, Patrik Reiske, Sole Traverso, Katharina Hohlbaum, Henning Sprekeler, Christa Th\"one-Reineke, Lars Lewejohann, Roman Bhuiyan

papers.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.

authors.name: Xilong Wang, Xiaoxing Chen, Neil Gong

papers.title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
papers.summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

authors.name: Songming Zhang, Yuxiao Luo, Shifu Luo, Siran Chen, Shuquan Su, Jinyan Li

papers.title: Condensing Law of Security Information
papers.summary: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.

authors.name: Qi Tan, Tianyu Cui, Qi Li, Ke Xu

papers.title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration
papers.summary: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.

authors.name: Bing Wang, Mingyang Wang, Yuanhang Mi, Yue Xu, Kaibo Su, Li'ang Xiao, Chunguo Wu, Changchun Li, Ximing Li, Kun-Feng Qiu, Bo Yang

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
papers.summary: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.

authors.name: Cosimo Galeone, Anna Ettorre, Ginevra Mariani, Minsu Park, Giuseppe Ettorre, Daniele Ligorio

papers.title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays
papers.summary: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.

authors.name: Weiru Zhang, Yuzhong Hong, Junwei Bao, Lemao Liu, Dejing Dou

papers.title: RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$: On-Device Reinforcement Learning Runtime
papers.summary: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on one embedded GPU shared with other workloads. Because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs stall the actor or let its policy drift. We present RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$, an on-device runtime that makes this coupling a tunable parameter: a refresh bound limits actor releases between refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritises the actor and fills spare time with training atop any base scheduler. Under the real refresh cost on two Jetson boards, RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$ keeps a 16.8 M-parameter policy's deadline misses below 1%, against 85 to 100% without it.

authors.name: Zexin Li, Xinwei Gao, Arvind Easwaran

papers.title: TelePhysica: Agentic Reconstruction of Physically Interactive Scenes
papers.summary: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.

authors.name: Ruiqi Shu, Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li

papers.title: AG-JEPA: Anatomically Guided Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Neurodegenerative Representation Learning
papers.summary: Brain MRI can reveal early signs of Alzheimers disease (AD) before measurable cognitive decline becomes apparent. However, during the transition from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), the disease-related signals are often subtle and confined to only a few brain regions. Existing Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models learn general structural representations but do not explicitly capture the anatomical regions affected in AD. We propose Anatomically Guided JEPA (AG-JEPA), which introduces anatomical tokens that interact with patch tokens during pretraining to learn region-specific representations from brain regions relevant to neurodegeneration. Building on this representation space, we further propose Prog-AG-JEPA, which models disease progression trajectory as a conditioned latent displacement within this space. We evaluate AG-JEPA across five downstream tasks spanning Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and progression prediction. AG-JEPA improves diagnosis and MCI prognosis, achieving an 8.4 percentage point AUROC gain over the strongest baseline on CN/MCI classification and a 7.1 percentage point gain on out-of-distribution CN/AD classification on the MR-RATE dataset, highlighting its effectiveness across both early-stage detection and cross-cohort generalization. For disease progression modeling, Prog-AG-JEPA consistently outperforms all baselines on future diagnosis and brain volume change prediction, demonstrating the value of anatomically grounded neurodegeneration representations for diagnosis and prognosis.

authors.name: Azad Singh, Ayantika Das, Amog Rao, Aiman Farooq, Anirban Porya, Ananya Shukla, Sowbhagya Suresh, Srinivasan Iyengar, Mohit Jain, Mercy Prasanna Ranjit

papers.title: EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
papers.summary: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

authors.name: Hongsen Cao, Shanxin Yuan, Mona Jaber, Ahmed Sayed

papers.title: An In-Silico Audit of Topographic Organization in a Multimodal Brain-Response Model
papers.summary: TRIBE v2 (d'Ascoli et al., 2026) predicts fMRI responses across the cortical surface from video, audio and text. Its authors validated it with category-selective localizers (faces, places, bodies, words) and language contrasts, but not with the classic topographic organization of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. There is a clear architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: TRIBE's video features are averaged over space before the response head, which should discard visual-field position. I present mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI mapping analyses, and a stand-in model with known ground truth that serves as a positive and negative control, and apply them to TRIBE v2's predictions, comparing the fitted maps with human atlases using spin tests. TRIBE v2 shows a sharp split. There is no contralateral hemifield response and no polar-angle map, robustly across stimulus controls. There is no tonotopic gradient in primary auditory cortex: best frequencies span an interquartile range of only 0.14 octaves across core and belt, and the null persists with loudness-equalized tones. An eccentricity-like gradient appears only when the ring geometry changes, consistent with global image statistics rather than a positional code. In contrast, motion selectivity is strong and precisely localized: 22% of the 1% most motion-selective vertices fall in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex. In-silico experiments that depend on feature identity appear viable with TRIBE v2, while those that depend on visual-field or frequency position are not supported by the current model.

authors.name: Jakub Strawa

papers.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models
papers.summary: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. LLM audits confirm the interpretability of the hand-crafted models. We first validate iWSP by tasking it with constructing transformers for canonical benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification, finding that LLM agents can successfully craft compact, accurate networks directly. Next, we apply iWSP to build neural encoding models across vision, language, and audition. In the visual cortex, iWSP outpredicts existing interpretable baselines, uncovers distinct computations across early/higher visual areas, and generalizes to unseen data. In language fMRI, iWSP surfaces a confound in the data and in auditory ECoG, it systematically discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict neural activity. Together, these results establish iWSP as a general paradigm for aligning high predictive performance with human-interpretable scientific discovery.

authors.name: Yash Mehta, Chandan Singh, Weijia Xu, Richard J. Antonello, Adeen Flinker, Nima Mesgarani, Michael F. Bonner, Nebojsa Jojic, Jianfeng Gao

papers.title: PUMA-Former: Uncertainty-Aware Agentic Computation Offloading in MEO-LEO Satellite Networks With Incomplete Information
papers.summary: Satellite edge computing distributes mobile workloads across moving processors whose service capacity must be coordinated over time. In medium Earth orbit (MEO)--low Earth orbit (LEO) networks, periodic reports leave CPU states stale or missing, making offloading sensitive to uncertain capacity and shared-destination congestion. We propose PUMA-Former, an uncertainty-aware agentic framework for cooperative offloading under incomplete information that balances completed work, service delay, and execution cost. A MEO coordinator maintains distinct-report memory and closes the loop between available evidence, capacity estimates, allocation commands, and execution feedback. Latent-delay attention weights plausible measurement-age hypotheses, and historical innovations refine CPU estimates around the latest received report. Queue-error-aware fusion incorporates auxiliary pressure while accounting for backlog uncertainty. The inferred resource moments condition a structured Transformer allocator for joint destination, partition, bandwidth, CPU, and power decisions. Bounded risk-aware calibration then adjusts workload splits to reflect uncertainty and shared destination load. In traffic-driven development evaluation, PUMA-Former increases admitted compute-work completion by 8.62%, reduces mean modeled service delay by 34.78%, and reduces mean episode-P95 delay by 71.08% relative to ATLA-adapt. It also improves completion and normalized energy over fixed-half round-robin offloading. Service gains over the learning baselines involve higher normalized energy.

authors.name: Yi Jing, Chunxiao Jiang, Jiawei Wang, Jiachen Sun

papers.title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

authors.name: Boming Yang, Yuquan Wang, Jiaxian Guo, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

papers.title: T2ST: Data-Efficient Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models via Temporal Data and Knowledge Transfer
papers.summary: Spatio-temporal foundation models (STFMs) require large-scale training corpora, yet synchronized observations and spatial metadata are costly to acquire and curate, limiting the availability of suitable data. By contrast, time-series data are abundant and easier to collect. Since observations at each location form a time series, this motivates a natural question: can abundant time-series data enhance STFMs when spatio-temporal observations are scarce? To bridge this gap, we propose T2ST, a data-efficient training framework that augments limited spatio-temporal observations with selected auxiliary time series and transfers knowledge from a frozen time-series foundation model. Our key insight is that temporal pattern learning can benefit from abundant external time series, while spatial dependency learning remains grounded in real spatio-temporal observations. Guided by this insight, T2ST retrieves matched sequences to reinforce sparsely observed temporal patterns and selects reliable complementary sequences to broaden temporal coverage. Temporal relation distillation aligns relationships among historical patches, while multi-scale prediction distillation transfers forecasting behavior at fine and coarse temporal resolutions, enabling knowledge transfer across heterogeneous architectures. Using only 10\% of the original spatio-temporal data, T2ST enables STFMs to achieve overall forecasting performance competitive with or superior to their full-data counterparts across six long-term and twelve short-term forecasting datasets. These results establish a new paradigm for data-efficient training of spatio-temporal foundation models. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/T2ST-65F3/.

authors.name: Yue Xu, Kaiyun Wei, Wenying Duan, Zichen Xu, Shuai Ma, Xiaoxi He

papers.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
papers.summary: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.

authors.name: Manas Mejari, Dario Piga, Marco Forgione

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.summary: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

authors.name: Mateusz Wozniak, Qi Gao, Agnieszka Wykowska

papers.title: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation
papers.summary: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity.
